Learning Objectives
Identify the basic biologic cascade surrounding shoulder osteoarthritis.
Acknowledge the unique contribution of instability to shoulder osteoarthritis.
Assess changes in non-cartilage tissues during shoulder osteoarthritis progression.
Specify the epidemiology and pathophysiology of glenohumeral osteoarthritis.
Perform an appropriate workup for patients in whom glenohumeral osteoarthritis is
suspected.

Basic Science
Epidemiology
Exceedingly common in many joints, including the glenohumeral joint
Increasing prevalence with increasing age
Correlation in research with multiple gene loci and proved in epidemiologic studies
Lifestyle factors may increase the risk of osteoarthritis.
Traumatic and postoperative osteoarthritis represent a small amount of shoulder
osteoarthritis cases.

Epidemiology
Osteoarthritis is associated with a massive financial burden on society, with United
States estimates ranging from $1,442 to $21,335 per patient.1,2 The number of total
shoulder arthroplasty (TSA) procedures has been increasing drastically in the United
States, with studies using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample predicting that shoulder
arthroplasty will be performed at a rate of 174,810 to 350,558 procedures per year by
2025, up from approximately 110,745 in 2017.2 This increase outpaces the rates of
increase of hip and knee arthroplasty by percentage.

the increasing incidence of clinically important shoulder osteoarthritis play a role. In
addition, advances in shoulder arthroplasty implants, an increasing numbers of
surgeons with fellowship training in shoulder surgery, and use of reverse arthroplasty
for previously unreconstructable shoulders have resulted in increased use. Figures 1
and 2 show two projected models of the volume of shoulder arthroplasty.2 Figure 3
specifically demonstrates the projected growth of anatomic TSA.2

Primary osteoarthritis may be genetically determined. Some genome-wide associated
scan studies have found 21 separate independent loci that increase susceptibility for
osteoarthritis.1 In addition, lifestyle choices and conditions, such as obesity and intensive
weight lifting, likely play some role in the development of osteoarthritis. Many studies
have associated obesity with an increased risk of knee osteoarthritis; however, similar
large-scale studies have not been conducted on the shoulder.
Traumatic and postoperative osteoarthritis also are observed in the clinical setting.
Because procedures have evolved and access and techniques have improved, the
incidence of osteoarthritis in these settings is difficult to predict.
Pathophysiology and Etiologies
Primary Osteoarthritis
Disease of the entire joint capsule, not just cartilage
Cascade is initiated by loss of hyaline cartilage integrity.
Periarticular tissues aid in reactive bone/osteophyte formation by influencing chondrocyte
activity.
Final common destination of the pathway is loss of articular surface, osteophyte formation,
and reactive changes in the periarticular tissues.

Primary Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis should be thought of as a disease of the entire joint. Components that are
involved include ligaments, capsule, synovial tissue, hyaline cartilage, and subchondral
bone. Periarticular musculature also is involved.
The instigating step for osteoarthritis progression is described as loss of hyaline cartilage
integrity. A structural/chemical change occurs in the makeup of the cartilage itself. This
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:41 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001178
5/64

makes the cartilage less wear resistant. Surface erosions begin to wear away the
cartilage because it is no longer able to maintain structural integrity.3
Periarticular tissues have a role in facilitating terminally differentiated chondrocyte
substrate synthesis upregulation. Multiple factors are produced, including matrix
metalloproteinase (MMP)-1, MMP-13, a disintegrin and metalloproteinase with
thrombospondin motifs (ADAMTS)-4, ADAMTS-5, interleukin-1, and other transforming
growth factors and tumor necrosis factors. Figure 4 helps visualize these changes.

plate via neurovascular channels and connect the subchondral bone with the overlying

= interleukin, MMP = matrix metalloproteinase, TGF = transforming growth factor, TNF =

R, et al: Osteoarthritis. Lancet 2015;385[9991]:376-387.)
Some of the substrates produce harmful effects on the surrounding tissues, including
other chondrocytes. This causes a more diffuse change in the entire joint milieu rather
than a pathology that can be thought of as solely affecting the articular surface.
The signalers also generate a mix of inflammatory and proliferative changes in the
surrounding synovium. The summative product is increased vascularity and increased
inflammation. Subchondral bone becomes more metabolically active, and vascular
invasion through the tide mark may be observed.3
Eventually this process leads to loss of the cartilage surface. In addition, osteophyte
formation is, in parallel, driven by chondral ossification and chondrocyte hyperactivity in
the periarticular regions. The final product is a joint surface devoid of cartilage and often
flanked by osteophyte formations.
Laboratory and Biochemical Signs
Low levels of synovial white blood cells (usually <2,000 cells/mm3 or <2 cells in 10 high-power
fields)
Increased ratio of chondroitin sulfate to keratin sulfate
Increased levels of collagenase
Most widely present osteoarthritis genetic predisposition is chromosome 2q with nodal
osteoarthritis

Laboratory and Biochemical Signs
Hallmarks of primary osteoarthritis include a loss of articular cartilage stiffness and an
increase in the water content (wet and mushy used to describe this change).
Osteoarthritic collagen will have an increased ratio of chondroitin sulfate to keratin
sulfate, which decreases in normal-aging cartilage. In a healthy infant, this ratio would be
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:41 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001178
8/64

greater than 10:1, but in a healthy adult, the ratio dwindles to 2:1. With osteoarthritis,
the ratio climbs back toward infantile levels.
Regarding cellular responses, chondrocytes cluster with late-stage arthritis. That
histologic finding is abnormal compared with cartilage with normal aging, in which fewer,
larger cells not in clusters are expected. Osteoarthritis collagen will have increased
collagenase presence with loss of organization of collagen fibrils. In normal aging,
increased cross-linking normally is observed.3
Aspirations of the osteoarthritic joint may be warranted to rule out other causes of
arthritis, such as inflammatory, crystalline, or infectious arthritis. The joint aspiration
associated with primary osteoarthritis is one devoid of large amounts of inflammatory
cells and existing in a culture-negative state.
Postcapsulorrhaphy Arthritis
Shoulder instability is a commonly encountered problem in many young patients.
Many procedures have been and are being performed to manage shoulder instability.
One well-described complication of these procedures, and a potential consequence of
recurrent instability, is glenohumeral arthritis, which may be caused by various patient,
pathologic, or technical factors.
Understanding these procedures, the residual anatomy, and the limitations imposed by the
previous surgical procedure is critical to providing adequate care for osteoarthritis in this
patient population.

Postcapsulorrhaphy Arthritis
Shoulder instability may be caused by physiologic laxity, poor dynamic control of the
glenohumeral joint, traumatic dislocation, or congenital difference. Many of these
patients may require surgical treatment to attain a stable shoulder. Procedures such as
the Latarjet procedure, Bristow procedure, Putti-Platt procedure, Bankart repair, or
other capsulorrhaphy may change the structural makeup of the shoulder.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:41 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001178
9/64

A well-known complication of these procedures is arthritis. Secondary arthritis may be
caused by graft malpositioning, overtightening, hardware malpositioning, intraoperative
iatrogenic articular damage, or thermal injury to the joint tissues.4 In addition, these
patients may have preexisting articular injury associated with the instability present
preoperatively.
These factors may ultimately cause the secondary form of glenohumeral arthritis.
Special considerations for these patients include altered anatomy because of soft-tissue
transfers or bony transfers, subscapularis quality, and remaining bone stock. Multiple
studies have written about the surgical challenges and overall positive outcomes of
shoulder arthroplasty in this patient population; however, it is important to acknowledge
them as a unique patient group. Recent studies demonstrate higher rates of
complications but improvement in pain and function with shoulder arthroplasty in this
patient population.4
Posttraumatic Arthritis
The pathophysiology may be directly proportional to how much force chondrocytes
experience.
A concentrated force of 20 to 40 MPa has been theorized to cause chondrocyte death.
Other factors, including MMP-3, ADAMTS-5, and tissue inhibitor of metallopeptidase-1, have
been identified as contributors to continued joint destruction after joint trauma.
Research on lubricin as a preventive treatment option is in its infancy but has shown promise
in some models.
These factors cause further chondrocyte apoptosis and may cause a positive feedback loop,
eventually generating widespread chondrocyte apoptosis.
This model suggests that after a critical number of chondrocytes has been destroyed, a self-
feeding positive feedback loop is generated, resulting in eventual widespread chondrocyte
death.

Posttraumatic Arthritis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:41 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001178
10/64

Posttraumatic arthritis may occur after one intra-articular injury. Therefore, a
considerable delay of decades may be present between the time of initial injury and the
diagnosis of arthritis. The pathogenesis of traumatic arthritis has been heavily studied.
Some data suggest that a direct concentrated cartilage impaction force of greater than
20 MPa may create direct chondrocyte death and a force of greater than 40 MPa is
almost certainly able to injure cartilage.
In a direct trauma model, chondrocyte initial mechanical destruction is contained to the
small margin of directly impacted chondrocytes. Wider joint damage may be attributed
to a less straightforward mechanism of injury. MMP-3, ADAMTS-5, tissue inhibitor of
metallopeptidase-1, and other factors may be introduced into the joint and have been
correlated with a risk of arthritis progression.5
Increased levels of many cytokines are observed after the acute post-chondrocyte injury
phase. Some literature has suggested that innate and adaptive immune responses also
may play a role in joint degeneration after trauma. Bone marrow lesions have been
described nearly ubiquitous after articular chondrocyte injury. Some research suggests
that cartilage overlying a bone marrow lesion from trauma may be abnormal years after
the injury and may predict long-term cartilage loss.1,5,6
Trauma also may affect periarticular blood supply and periarticular kinematics, which
may hasten osteoarthritis progression. Some research has been focused on secondary
prevention, and lubricin has shown some promise in animal and benchtop models;
however, a unified and well-proven treatment option to prevent osteoarthritis past
appropriate surgical management in this patient population does not appear to exist.
Pain Generation in Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis pain may be associated with pain in the morning or after periods of rest.
Specifically in the shoulder, pain and limitations with internal and external rotation are
common.
Crepitation and crepitation associated with pain may be present.
In other joints, bone marrow lesions have been correlated with pain level.
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001178
11/64

In glenohumeral osteoarthritis, the degree of radiographic severity may not correlate with self-
assessed shoulder comfort and function.

Pain Generation in Osteoarthritis
Patients with osteoarthritis may have pain in the morning or after long periods of rest.
They may associate pain with joint crepitation or swelling. Pain also may be directly
associated with increased loading of the joint. Forceful motions causing osteophytes on
articular contact also may generate pain, which occasionally can be observed with
external rotation in primary osteoarthritic shoulders. Peripheral nociceptive receptors
exposed to higher levels of stimulation and previous inflammatory mediators may
sensitize the joint to pain.1,3 This pain and sensitization may create a self-feeding pain-
intensifying cycle. This and the chronic nature of osteoarthritis (ie, its irreversible
presence) may act as a driver of chronic pain in osteoarthritis.
Radiographic findings and advanced disease may not necessarily predict overall patient
comfort or function. This correlation has been evaluated preoperatively in patients
undergoing shoulder arthroplasty. Matsen et al7 reported on more than 500 patients
and found that those with more severe radiographic arthritis (more retroversion, B
glenoids, and decentering) did not have lower self-assessed comfort and function scores
compared with other patients.
MRI evaluations of possible reasons for more painful or less painful osteoarthritis have
been performed. More commonly studied in the knee, a correlation between the
amount of synovitis and bone marrow lesions has been described. Some research
supports a strong correlation between pain in proportion with the amount of synovitis
and increasing bone marrow lesions observed on MRI.3
Osteoarthritis
Epidemiology

Primary osteoarthritis: age-related loss of articular cartilage that often affects healthy and
active patients
Secondary causes of osteoarthritis
Posttraumatic
Capsulorrhaphy arthropathy
Rotator cuff tear arthropathy
Osteonecrosis

Epidemiology
Damage to the humeral head or glenoid cartilage may lead to articular incongruity and
progression of arthritis. In addition, malunion or nonunion of the tuberosities may lead
to abnormal joint kinematics that may subsequently lead to loss of concentric motion
and preferential cartilage wear.
Capsulorrhaphy arthropathy is a complication of previous surgery for glenohumeral
instability in combination with overtightening of the joint capsule and prominent suture
anchors, staples, screws, or transferred coracoid bone that causes damage to the
humeral articular surface.
A torn rotator cuff loses its ability to compress the humeral head into the glenoid,
leading to superior translation of the humeral head. This may lead to superior wear of
the glenoid and acetabularization of the undersurface of the acromion.
Pathophysiology
Begins with joint space narrowing and subchondral sclerosis from articular cartilage wear
As the disease process progresses, subchondral cysts and humeral and glenoid osteophytes
form.
Primary glenohumeral osteoarthritis typically occurs in one of two patterns:
Concentric medial loss
Eccentric posterior wear

Posterior glenoid wear and posterior humeral head subluxation occur in as many as 45% of
shoulders affected by primary osteoarthritis (Resource 1).
Full-thickness rotator cuff tears rarely (5% to 10%) are associated with primary osteoarthritis.

Pathophysiology
Joint space narrowing and periarticular osteophyte formation most commonly occur on
the inferior aspects of the humeral head, and the result has been referred to as a goat’s
beard (Figures 5 and 6).

humeral head is concentrically located (Walch type A2 glenoid). In addition, a type III
acromion and a large inferior humeral osteophyte with the typical goat’s beard shape
(arrow in panel A) are noted. (Reproduced from Petri M, Greenspoon JA, Millett PJ:

388.)

Posterior eccentric wear causes pathologic changes that lead to additional posterior
subluxation of the humeral head. As the humeral head subluxates posteriorly, the
articular contact area decreases and causes increased contact pressure, further
increasing posterior wear (Figure 7). This may lead to a biconcavity with formation of a
neo-glenoid and acquired glenoid retroversion. As posterior glenoid wear and humeral
head subluxation increase, the anterior soft tissues, including the anterior capsule and
the subscapularis, become contracted, limiting external rotation and further increasing
the tendency of the humeral head to translate posteriorly.

Evaluation
Patient History
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Shoulder Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001178

Common symptoms include pain with activity, pain at night, decreased range of motion, and
loss of function.
A history of trauma, instability, or joint surgery should be elicited for possible secondary
causes of osteoarthritis.

Patient History
Pain often is reported to be diffuse or deep in the joint; however, patients often localize
the worst pain in the posterior aspect of the shoulder. Although the pain may begin as
related to strenuous activity, it may progress to pain with any shoulder movement and
be present at rest or at night. Range of motion becomes progressively limited and
inhibits activities of daily living, such as dressing, combing hair, and reaching overhead
(Resource 2).
Physical Examination
Common physical examination findings include crepitus; painful motion; and limited active
and passive range of motion, especially external rotation.

Physical Examination
Anterior soft-tissue flattening and prominence of the coracoid process secondary to
posterior subluxation may be observed. Because of inactivity, muscle atrophy also may
be noted about the entire shoulder girdle, especially about the anterior deltoid. An
important finding is limited active and passive range of motion rather than only limited
active range of motion with preserved passive range of motion, which is more consistent
with a rotator cuff tear/pseudoparalysis. Rotator cuff strength usually is preserved but
may be difficult to assess because of limitations in passive motion.
Imaging Studies

Radiographs—AP, true glenohumeral AP (Grashey), and axillary views should be obtained.
A CT scan may provide additional information on bony changes of the glenohumeral joint.
Advanced CT software can be used for three-dimensional preoperative planning of glenoid
reaming and implant placement.
MRI may provide additional information about the soft tissues, such as the rotator cuff, if
clinical concerns exist.
Common radiographic findings include symmetric or asymmetric joint space narrowing,
subchondral sclerosis, and osteophytes about the glenoid and the humeral head (Figure 8).
Posterior glenoid erosion (also known as a biconcave glenoid) with humeral head subluxation
may be evident on axillary radiographs (Figure 9).
An AP radiograph in the plane of the scapula (Grashey view) is necessary to evaluate coronal
alignment of the glenohumeral joint and evaluate for osteophytes, joint space narrowing, and
proximal humeral migration (Figure 10).

Management/Therapy
Nonsurgical Management
NSAIDs may afford symptomatic relief by decreasing associated inflammation; however, the
potential benefit of these medications must be weighed against their known adverse effects,
such as gastrointestinal bleeding and kidney injury.
Physical therapy and activity modifications
Intra-articular glenohumeral corticosteroid injection may afford substantial, but likely
temporary, relief. Data on the effectiveness of intra-articular corticosteroid injections are
limited, and information mostly is extrapolated from literature on the knee joint.
Other intra-articular injectable solutions are available, such as hyaluronic acid, stem cells, and
platelet-rich plasma; however, the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons Evidence-
Based Clinical Practice Guideline on the Management of Glenohumeral Joint Arthritis does not
recommend their use because of lack of reliable evidence (Resource 3).

Nonsurgical Management
Gentle stretching exercises may improve or prevent worsening of stiffness related to
contracture and adhesions involving the capsule, rotator cuff muscles, and
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 10:41 AM
AAOS | Shoulder Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001178
22/64

humeroscapular motion interface. Gentle periscapular muscle strengthening may help
with deconditioning and provide stabilization in patients with posterior subluxation;
however, aggressive stretching and heavy weight training may exacerbate symptoms.
Strenuous activities that involve impact loading and lifting heavy weight may accelerate
the progression of arthritis. Minimizing these activities may decrease dysfunction and
prolong maintenance of the patient’s native joint. Modifying activity and focusing on low-
impact sports, such as rowing and swimming, likely will be better tolerated.
Surgical Management
Indications: persistent symptoms despite nonsurgical management; symptoms causing
substantial disability and dysfunction that affect a patient’s capacity to perform activities of
daily living
Arthroscopy: may include removal of osteophytes, capsular release, loose body removal,
chondroplasty, synovectomy, and/or axillary nerve neurolysis.
Hemiarthroplasty: pain relief and range of motion generally are good but are less predictable
than after TSA.
TSA: a metallic humeral head and a cemented all-polyethylene glenoid prosthesis provides the
most reliable pain relief and functionality.

Surgical Management
Synovectomy may be appropriate in patients with active synovitis and mild articular
disease. This treatment option is most beneficial during the early stages of the disease,
before joint destruction. The duration and efficacy of pain relief depend on the severity
of the disease. Typically, arthroscopic synovectomy is preferred over open synovectomy
to reduce morbidity and because it allows for improved visualization of the entire joint
space.13 If the rotator cuff tendon is torn and cannot be repaired, the coracoacromial
arch should be preserved to prevent anterosuperior escape of the humeral head.
Historically, hemiarthroplasty has been indicated for patients with advanced disease
who have a massive, irreparable rotator cuff tear; however, recently, reverse TSA has
been used for this indication. Hemiarthroplasty still may be appropriate if bone stock is
inadequate to support a glenoid prosthesis and overhead active motion is maintained.
TSA requires adequate bone stock to support a glenoid prosthesis, and the rotator cuff
must be intact or have a small tear that is repairable. Frequently, reverse TSA is
preferred over TSA because of the higher risk for rotator cuff failure in patients with
inflammatory arthropathy. Contraindications include active infection, a nonfunctioning
deltoid muscle, a nonfunctioning or insufficient rotator cuff, an irreparable rotator cuff
tear, brachial plexus palsy, and severe glenoid bone loss. Overall outcomes are good to
excellent but slightly inferior compared with those in patients with osteoarthritis.
Ideally, reverse TSA is indicated in patients with rotator cuff arthropathy who have poor
forward elevation; however, reverse TSA also is indicated in elderly patients with
inflammatory arthritis who have a compromised rotator cuff. The glenoid bone stock
must be adequate to support a prosthesis. In addition, patients must have a functional
axillary nerve and deltoid muscle. The overall outcomes generally are good to
excellent.14

Knowledge of this classification system is necessary to inform surgical treatment

transects the humeral head. Type B glenoids demonstrate posterior humeral head

posterior glenoid bony erosion. Type B2 is posterior head subluxation with posterior


Anatomic TSA
Anatomic and reverse TSA are the most commonly performed definitive treatment
options for glenohumeral arthritis and are associated with pain relief, improved
function, and patient satisfaction in approximately 95% of patients.58 Implant
survivorship is estimated to be higher than 85% at 15-year follow-up.59 Substantial
posterior bone loss (type B2, type B3, and type C glenoids) leads to increased joint line
medialization, glenoid retroversion, and posterior subluxation of the humeral head,
making these cases challenging to manage.
Posterior bone loss may contribute to glenoid component malpositioning and loosening
secondary to inadequate bone support and suboptimal glenoid component seating.60,61
Placement of a glenoid component in more than 10° of retroversion has been shown to
increase component micromotion and stress,62 and glenoid component malpositioning
frequently is present in patients in whom TSA fails.63 Glenoid component retroversion of
more than 15° also has been correlated with increased rates of osteolysis around the
implant.64 Therefore, several surgical techniques have been developed to restore the
normal glenohumeral joint line and glenoid version during anatomic TSA, including
eccentric glenoid reaming, use of bone graft, and use of augmented glenoid
components. Data supports the use of standard implants placed in retroversion, with
good short-term outcomes.65,66 Longer term studies are necessary to determine
whether a superior technique exists with standard components.

create a stable implant, and achieve full backside support of the glenoid component
(Figure 19). The goal is to create a congruent contact between the bone and the glenoid
prosthesis and a neutral articulation between the glenoid and the humeral implants.60
The amount of glenoid version that may be corrected via this method is limited by
diminished bony support of the glenoid component in correction of more substantial
retroversion and component peg perforation. For example, correction of 15° of

Reverse TSA
Although reverse TSA is commonly performed to manage rotator cuff arthropathy, it
does have a role in the management of rotator cuff–intact osteoarthritic shoulders.
Reverse TSA usually is reserved for patients with severe glenoid bone deficits in whom
bone stock and soft-tissue balancing are concerns.25 Although reverse TSA has shown
good short-, intermediate-, and long-term patient-reported outcomes, evidence suggests
that younger patients (<60 years) report lower satisfaction with reverse TSA;79 however,
this has not been specifically investigated in the use of reverse TSA for the management
of primary glenohumeral arthritis in patients with severe glenoid bone loss. Reverse TSA
without bone grafting has demonstrated substantial improvement in patient-reported
outcomes and reliable short-term implant survivorship if performed in patients with
severe osteoarthritis and substantial glenoid bone loss who have an intact rotator cuff.80
Similar to anatomic TSA, reverse TSA can be performed in combination with glenoid
bone grafting to restore bone stock if severe deformity is present,81 resulting in reliable
functional results and good patient-reported outcomes;82-84 however, a high incidence
of baseplate loosening also has been reported.85 Bone grafting can be performed in
combination with methods that maximize purchase of reverse TSA baseplate central
screw or peg, such as use of the alternate scapular spine centerline in patients with
severe bone loss. This technique places the baseplate central screw/peg along the axis of
the scapular spine and its junction with the body of the scapula to increase bony

Hemiarthroplasty
Hemiarthroplasty for the management of glenohumeral arthritis may be an option in younger
patients with higher demand jobs or lifestyles.
Hemiarthroplasty in combination with glenoid reaming without prosthetic resurfacing has
been advocated by some studies.

Hemiarthroplasty
The advantage of hemiarthroplasty is avoiding the most common complication in
anatomic TSA: glenoid component loosening. Some studies have advocated performing
a hemiarthroplasty with bony recontouring (concentric reaming) of the glenoid. This
technique often is reserved for young and/or highly active patients who have a
substantial risk for glenoid component loosening. Previous literature has documented
the superiority of anatomic TSA versus hemiarthroplasty with regard to pain and
function;89 however, some patients may be willing to accept less reliable pain relief for
maintenance of a higher level of activity. The bony recontouring technique with
hemiarthroplasty has been described as a treatment option for type B2 morphology, in
which the glenoid biconcavity is reamed to a single concavity to reestablish normal
glenohumeral contact forces, and has been termed the ream-and-run technique90
(Figure 24). If performed in patients with type B2 glenoid morphology, a low rate of
revision, improved humeral head centering, and improved patient-reported outcomes at
midterm follow-up have been reported.91 Potential disadvantages of hemiarthroplasty
via the ream-and-run technique include progressive glenoid erosion, glenoid-sided
arthritic pain, and recurrent instability.92 In addition, some studies have not
demonstrated the reported successes92 previously reported with this technique, and
these results may be surgeon and patient dependent.

Summary
The Walch classification provides surgeons with a tool to communicate glenoid morphology
and bone loss in patients with glenohumeral osteoarthritis.
However, various treatment techniques are available for each Walch type, depending on
patient factors (age, activity level, etc.), bony factors (glenoid morphology and glenohumeral
relationships), and soft-tissue factors (rotator cuff status).
Few prospective comparative studies are available on treatment options for the management
of Walch type; as additional preoperative morphology data are published, the importance of
